Are there any systems inulase to prevent sewage backup?
Since the average sewage/waste water system are old and outdated and most people ate staying home is there a high chance of raw sewage backup?

Short answer: No.

Longer Answer: There are no separate systems for commercial or residential zones. All sewer and storm drainage go to the same plant. If the plant is overburdened they just divert the excess to a river or a contained flood plane in certain areas.

The people with septic systems might have some problems.

As I understand it, the sewage systems are in pretty good shape. When there's a problem with the waste water systems it causes a lot of damage and a lot of complaints so they're kept up pretty well. The actual storage and teratment of the wastewater is centeralized so that won't be overwhelmed because it all ends up there whether it's from commercial or residential sources. The system to transport the sewage from the residences to the treatment facilities is built to handle peak volume. When there are backups it tends to be from flooding in areas with a high water level, or if there's damage to the pipe between a house and the street like if tree roots grow into it.

What you might hear about sewage systems getting overwhelmed is probably from large urban areas that have a mixed stormsewer and sanitary sewer system. The transportation pipes are separate, but they both get dumped into giant underground storage facilities to await treatment. In the summer you'll sometimes read about a large city discharging hundreds of thousands of gallons of "untreated sewage" into a large body of water. Because it's a mixed system, most of what is being discharged is rain runoff. It's true that it's contaminated with untreated waste water, but they're not discharging pure sewage like the newspaper headlines make it sound.

Plumberfag here. Some municipalities are experiencing problems, not necessarily due to the increased residential load but because of an increase in wipes and other things (t-shirts, rags, etc.) being flushed down the toilet that shouldn’t be. That causes problems with lift stations (where the sewage has to be pumped out). A modern lift station will have macerating pumps that can grind up wipes, tampons, etc. However rags and t-shirts can still bind them up, and too many wipes can bind the pumps as well. Also most municipalities use concrete pipe for larger sewer/storm drains. Roots can start to grow where the pipe is damaged or at a joint that is starting to fail. Wipes and rags will get caught in the root bundle and won’t disintegrate, so most cities have a maintenance schedule to clear roots and to hydro the lines. More wipes = more backups, and sometimes the backups can be bad enough that they will backup into a home and flood it with sewage. Some homes and buildings located in vulnerable areas will install backwater valves on their sewer main, which is basically a check valve designed to stop a backup in the city from coming back into the building. These have their own problems, however, as TP can get caught in the check valve and the backwater valve can actually be the cause of a backup in many circumstances.
